building-eval-datasets.title: Creating Eval Datasets: Sourcing, Labeling, and Versioning

sections.title: Why Your Eval Dataset Makes or Breaks Everything
sections.content:
Here's the thing — you can have the most elegant rubric in the world, but if your eval dataset doesn't match what users actually throw at your product, you're testing the wrong thing. The dataset is where theory meets reality. I've seen teams spend weeks tuning prompts against a beautifully curated dataset of edge cases, only to discover their production traffic looks nothing like it.

From what I've observed, the best eval datasets come from four complementary sources: production logs (what users actually ask), human annotation (domain experts labeling quality), synthetic generation (programmatically creating edge cases), and domain-specific knowledge bases (grounding truth for factual queries). Teresa Torres documented this when building Product Talk's Interview Coach AI — she started with real user transcripts, then systematically added adversarial cases where the AI might hallucinate or get tone wrong.

The goal isn't perfection. It's representativeness. Your eval dataset should reflect the distribution of production queries — the common cases that make up 80% of traffic, plus the edge cases that cause 80% of your support tickets. (Quality beats quantity every time.)

sections.question: You're building an eval dataset for a customer support chatbot. Your dataset currently has 200 carefully written test cases covering common queries like password resets and order status. Users report the bot fails on complex returns involving multiple items. What's the best next step?

options.text: Add 200 more synthetic cases to double the dataset size
Sample production logs for actual multi-item return queries and add those edge cases to the dataset
Increase the passing score threshold to catch more failures
Switch from human evaluation to LLM-as-judge for faster iteration

sections.explanation: The dataset needs to reflect the production distribution where the AI is failing. Sampling real multi-item return queries ensures your evals test the actual edge cases users encounter. Simply adding more synthetic cases or changing scoring won't help if you're not testing the right scenarios.

sections.title: Labeling: Getting from Raw Data to Ground Truth
sections.content:
Once you've sourced a batch of queries, you need labels — the ground truth that tells you whether a response is good or not. This is where things get messy. What counts as 'good' is often subjective, especially for open-ended tasks like summarization or creative writing.

Hamel Husain's field guide emphasizes something crucial: measure inter-annotator agreement using metrics like Cohen's κ (kappa) or Krippendorff's α. If two human raters disagree 40% of the time on what makes a good response, you don't have a labeling problem — you have a rubric problem. Go back and tighten your criteria until agreement is above 80%. (This is why we spent the last module building explicit rubrics.)

For specialized domains, LLM-as-judge hits a wall. Aman Khan's research with Arize AI shows that while strong LLM judges reach 80-90% agreement with humans on general tasks, that drops to 60-70% on expert domains like medical advice or legal reasoning. Use LLM judges for scalable initial screening, then route uncertain or high-stakes cases to human experts. It's a workflow, not an either-or.

sections.title: Inter-annotator agreement is your canary
sections.content: If your labelers disagree frequently, your rubric isn't clear enough. Fix the rubric first — no amount of data or fancy tooling will save you from ambiguous criteria.

sections.question: Match each labeling scenario to the most appropriate evaluation approach:

pairs.left: Screening 10,000 customer support responses for tone violations
Verifying medical diagnosis accuracy for a clinical AI assistant
Testing if code compiles and passes unit tests

sections.explanation: The right evaluation approach depends on scale, stakes, and domain expertise required. LLM judges scale for high-volume, lower-stakes tasks. Human experts are essential when accuracy requires specialized knowledge. Deterministic checks work when success is objectively verifiable.

sections.title: Versioning: Treating Your Dataset Like Production Code
sections.content:
Let's get real — your dataset will change. User behavior shifts, your product adds features, edge cases emerge from production. If you're not versioning your eval dataset, you have no idea whether a score drop means your model got worse or your dataset got harder.

Implement version control the same way you would for code. Tag each dataset version with a date and change summary. When you add 50 new edge cases for multi-item returns, that's v1.2. When you remove 30 obsolete queries because you deprecated a feature, that's v1.3. Track scores against each version so you can compare apples to apples.

From what I've seen, successful teams schedule quarterly dataset reviews. They sample recent production logs, check if the eval distribution still matches reality, and prune test cases that no longer matter. Andrej Karpathy has talked about this in the context of Tesla's self-driving evals — the dataset has to evolve as the product and real-world conditions change, otherwise you're optimizing for yesterday's problems.

sections.title: Trip-planning agent dataset evolution
sections.content: When building evals for a travel booking agent answering queries like 'relaxing weekend near SF under $1,000', the team started with 200 cases. After launch, production logs revealed users often asked about pet-friendly options — missing from the original dataset. They added 40 pet-related queries in v1.1, then later added 30 international travel cases in v1.2 when that feature launched. Each version was tagged and scored separately to track progress.

sections.statement: If your model's eval score drops from 85% to 78% after adding 100 new test cases to the dataset, it means the model has regressed and needs immediate fixes.
sections.explanation: Not necessarily. The score drop could simply reflect that the new test cases are harder or cover edge cases the model hasn't been tuned for. This is why versioning matters — you need to compare scores on the same dataset version over time to detect true regression. A harder dataset should be treated as v2.0, and you'd evaluate both versions separately.

points: Your eval dataset must reflect production distribution — source from real logs, add edge cases, and prune obsolete queries regularly.
Measure inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ or Krippendorff's α above 80%) to ensure your labeling rubric is clear enough.
Use LLM-as-judge for scalable screening on general tasks, but route specialized or high-stakes decisions to human experts.
Version your datasets like code — tag changes, track scores per version, and schedule quarterly reviews to keep evals relevant.

flashcards.front: What are the four complementary sources for building a representative eval dataset?
flashcards.back: Production logs (real user queries), human annotation (expert quality labels), synthetic generation (programmatic edge cases), and domain-specific knowledge bases (factual grounding).

flashcards.front: What is inter-annotator agreement and why does it matter for eval datasets?
flashcards.back: Inter-annotator agreement (measured by Cohen's κ or Krippendorff's α) quantifies how consistently human raters label the same data. If agreement is below 80%, your rubric criteria are too ambiguous and need tightening before you scale labeling.

flashcards.front: When should you use LLM-as-judge versus human evaluation for labeling?
flashcards.back: Use LLM-as-judge for scalable initial screening on general tasks (80-90% human agreement). Use human experts for specialized domains, high-stakes decisions, or nuanced judgment where LLM agreement drops to 60-70%.

flashcards.front: Why must eval datasets be versioned and regularly updated?
flashcards.back: User behavior changes, products add features, and edge cases emerge. Versioning lets you track whether score changes reflect true model regression or dataset difficulty shifts. Schedule quarterly reviews to keep the dataset aligned with production.

flashcards.front: What does it mean for an eval dataset to reflect 'production distribution'?
flashcards.back: The dataset should mirror the mix of queries users actually send — both the common cases making up 80% of traffic and the edge cases causing 80% of failures. Quality and representativeness beat raw dataset size.

human-vs-llm-judges.title: Human Graders vs. LLM-as-Judge: Trade-offs and When to Use Each

sections.title: The Core Trade-off: Speed vs. Nuance
sections.content:
Here's the thing — when you're building evals for an AI product, one of your first decisions is who (or what) actually scores the outputs. You can hire human graders who bring judgment and expertise. Or you can use another LLM to judge the first one's work, which is fast and scales. From what I've seen, most teams need both, just at different stages.

LLM-as-judge systems achieve 80-90% agreement with humans on general tasks — things like summarization, tone, basic question-answering. That drops to 60-70% when the domain gets specialized or nuanced. Hamel Husain's field guide emphasizes this calibration step: you run LLM judges alongside humans on a sample, measure agreement, and decide where automation makes sense. If you're evaluating a customer support chatbot's politeness, an LLM judge will probably do fine. If you're checking whether a radiology AI correctly identified a rare tumor feature, you need a radiologist.

The trap is thinking it's purely a cost question. LLM judges are scalable, but at high volume API costs add up, and systematic biases creep in — self-preference (favoring outputs from the same model family), position bias (preferring the first option shown), verbosity bias (longer answers score higher). You still need humans to spot those patterns.

sections.question: Match each evaluation scenario to the most appropriate judge type:

pairs.left: Screening 10,000 chatbot responses for basic tone compliance
Validating legal contract clause accuracy in specialized domain
Running nightly regression checks on prompt changes
Evaluating medical diagnosis suggestions for rare conditions

sections.explanation: LLM judges excel at high-volume, general tasks where speed and consistency matter — tone checks, regression tests, initial screening. Humans are essential when the domain requires specialized knowledge, when stakes are high (medical, legal), or when you need to catch subtle errors that correlate with real-world harm. The pattern: automate the broad filter, bring in humans for the edge cases and expertise-heavy calls.

sections.title: When LLM Judges Work (and When They Don't)
sections.content:
Let's get practical. LLM judges shine in three situations: when you need to evaluate hundreds or thousands of outputs quickly, when the rubric is clear and the task is general (summarization quality, following formatting rules), and when you're running continuous regression checks in CI/CD. Teresa Torres documented this for Product Talk's Interview Coach — they used GPT-4 as a judge to score coaching feedback on dimensions like specificity and actionability, running evals nightly to catch prompt drift.

But LLM judges struggle with subjective judgment, specialized expertise, and adversarial cases. I've seen teams try to use LLM-as-judge for creative writing quality or brand voice alignment — it correlates poorly with what actual users like. Aman Khan's course with Andrew Ng walks through calibration: you take a sample of 100–200 cases, score them with both humans and LLMs, calculate agreement (Cohen's kappa), and only proceed if you're above 0.7 or so. Below that, you're measuring something different than what humans care about.

One more thing: LLM judges can be gamed. If your production model learns (through fine-tuning or prompt tweaking) that longer answers score higher with the judge, you'll inflate scores without improving real quality. You need periodic human spot-checks to validate that high LLM-judge scores still correlate with good user outcomes.

sections.title: Watch for Self-Preference Bias
sections.content: If you use GPT-4 to judge GPT-4 outputs, it systematically favors its own style and phrasing. When comparing models, use a neutral third-party judge or rotate judge models to catch this bias. I've seen teams confidently ship a worse model because their eval setup had hidden self-preference baked in.

sections.question: Your team is evaluating a legal document AI that generates contract clauses. LLM-as-judge scores are 90% on average, but lawyers report frequent subtle errors. What's the most likely issue?

options.text: The LLM judge is suffering from position bias and favoring the first clause shown.
The task requires specialized legal expertise that general LLM judges lack, so agreement with experts is only 60-70%.
The dataset is too small to detect meaningful differences in performance.
The LLM judge needs its temperature set to zero for reproducibility.

sections.explanation: This is a classic case of domain specialization. LLM judges achieve 80-90% agreement on general tasks but drop to 60-70% on expert domains like law or medicine. The high average score from the LLM judge is misleading — it's measuring surface fluency, not legal correctness. You need human legal experts to catch the subtle errors that matter. Position bias (a) affects preference ordering, not accuracy detection. Temperature (d) affects consistency, not expertise. Sample size (c) isn't the issue when experts consistently find errors.

sections.title: Building a Hybrid Workflow That Scales
sections.content:
From what I've observed, the teams that ship reliably use a two-stage funnel. LLM judges do the first pass — they're your high-volume filter, catching obvious failures (formatting errors, tone violations, hallucinations you can detect with reference docs). Then humans review a stratified sample: the worst-scoring outputs (where the model struggled), a random sample from the middle (to check for blind spots), and a few top-scorers (to validate that high scores mean what you think).

Hamel Husain calls this the calibration loop. You're not replacing humans — you're using automation to decide where human attention goes. If your LLM judge flags 200 outputs as risky out of 10,000, you review those 200 plus maybe 50 random others. That's 250 human judgments instead of 10,000, and you've probably caught 90% of the real issues.

One more piece: use human reviews to improve your LLM judge. When humans disagree with the LLM on a case, that's signal. Add those disagreements to your calibration set, refine your judge prompt or rubric, re-run agreement metrics. Over time, your LLM judge gets better at predicting what your humans (and users) actually care about. This is the flywheel Aman Khan talks about — production data informs datasets, datasets power evals, evals surface disagreements, disagreements improve prompts.

sections.statement: LLM-as-judge is always cheaper than human evaluation because API calls cost less than hiring graders.
sections.explanation: Not always. While LLM judges scale easily, at high volume the API costs add up — especially if you're using GPT-4 or Claude to judge thousands of outputs daily. More importantly, LLM judges have systematic biases and blind spots, so you still need periodic human review to validate that scores correlate with real quality. The cost advantage is real for initial screening, but 'always cheaper' misses the hidden costs of bias, miscalibration, and the human oversight you still need.

sections.title: Start with Small-Scale Calibration
sections.content: Before running LLM-as-judge at scale, score 100–200 outputs with both humans and your LLM judge, then calculate Cohen's kappa. If agreement is below 0.7, dig into where they diverge — you might need to refine your rubric, add examples to the judge prompt, or accept that this task needs more human involvement. This 2-hour investment saves weeks of chasing misleading metrics.

points: LLM judges achieve 80-90% agreement with humans on general tasks but only 60-70% in expert domains — calibrate before you scale.
Use LLM-as-judge for high-volume screening and continuous regression checks; bring in humans for nuanced judgment, high-stakes decisions, and specialized expertise.
Build a two-stage funnel: LLM judges filter at scale, humans review worst cases plus stratified samples to validate and catch blind spots.
LLM judges have systematic biases — self-preference, position bias, verbosity bias — so periodic human review is essential even when automation works.
Use disagreements between LLM and human judges to refine your rubric and improve calibration over time.

flashcards.front: What is the typical agreement rate between LLM judges and humans on general tasks vs. expert domains?
flashcards.back: LLM judges achieve 80-90% agreement with humans on general tasks (like summarization or tone), but only 60-70% agreement in specialized expert domains (like legal or medical evaluation). This gap means you need human experts when domain knowledge is critical.

flashcards.front: What are the three main systematic biases that LLM-as-judge systems exhibit?
flashcards.back: Self-preference bias (favoring outputs from the same model family), position bias (preferring options shown first), and verbosity bias (scoring longer answers higher regardless of quality). These biases require periodic human validation to detect.

flashcards.front: Describe the two-stage hybrid evaluation funnel that scales effectively.
flashcards.back: First stage: LLM judges screen all outputs at high volume, flagging obvious failures. Second stage: humans review worst-scoring outputs, a random middle sample, and some top-scorers to validate. This focuses expensive human attention where it matters most while maintaining coverage.

flashcards.front: When should you use LLM-as-judge vs. human evaluation?
flashcards.back: Use LLM judges for: high-volume screening, clear rubrics on general tasks, continuous regression testing. Use humans for: specialized expertise, subjective judgment, high-stakes decisions, catching adversarial cases, and validating that LLM scores correlate with real user outcomes.

flashcards.front: What is Cohen's kappa and why does it matter for LLM-as-judge calibration?
flashcards.back: Cohen's kappa measures inter-rater agreement between your LLM judge and human graders. Values above 0.7 indicate good alignment. You calculate it on 100-200 sample cases before scaling LLM judges to ensure they're measuring what humans (and users) actually care about.

flashcards.front: How do you use disagreements between LLM and human judges to improve your eval system?
flashcards.back: When humans and LLM judges disagree on a case, add it to your calibration set. Analyze the pattern of disagreements to refine your rubric, add clarifying examples to the judge prompt, or adjust scoring criteria. This creates a feedback loop where your LLM judge gets better at predicting human judgment over time.

interpreting-eval-results.title: Reading Eval Results: Aggregate Scores, Distributions, and Regressions

sections.title: Why Averages Lie to You
sections.content:
Here's the thing — when you first run an eval, you'll see a single number at the top of the dashboard: average score 7.2/10. Your instinct is to declare victory or sound the alarm. From what I've seen, that's exactly where most PMs go wrong.

The mean score hides the shape of what's happening. Maybe 80% of your responses are perfect 9s and 10s, but 20% are complete failures scoring 1 or 2. That averages to a respectable 7.6, but you've shipped a product that catastrophically fails one in five times. Or maybe everything clusters around 7 — mediocre across the board, no disasters but nothing great either. Same average, completely different product reality.

What you actually need is the distribution. Look at the histogram. Where do scores cluster? How fat is the tail of terrible responses? Are there bimodal peaks suggesting the model handles some query types beautifully and others not at all? (I've seen teams ship features based on a good average score, only to discover in production that a specific user segment was getting systematically bad responses the whole time.)

sections.question: Your travel booking agent scores an average of 7.8/10 on helpfulness. When you examine the distribution, you find 70% of responses score 9-10, and 30% score 3-4. What does this pattern suggest about your product readiness?

options.text: The product is ready to ship because the average exceeds 7.5
You have a systematic failure mode affecting nearly a third of queries that needs investigation before launch
The distribution is normal and expected for AI systems, so no action is needed
You should focus on improving the high-scoring responses to push the average above 8.0

sections.explanation: A bimodal distribution with 30% of responses scoring 3-4 indicates a systematic problem — likely a specific query type, edge case, or user intent the model can't handle. Shipping this means roughly one in three users gets a poor experience. The average masks this critical failure mode. You need to identify what triggers the low scores (query patterns, missing knowledge, tone mismatches) and fix it before launch.

sections.title: Three Levels of Reading: Mean, Distribution, Examples
sections.content:
I think of eval results as having three layers you need to read through — each one gets you closer to what's actually broken (or working).

First layer: mean scores per criterion. Not just overall average, but broken down by each rubric dimension. Your chatbot might score 8.5 on tone but 5.2 on factual accuracy. That tells you where to focus. Second layer: score distributions and patterns. Group results by query type, user segment, or response length. Does the model fail consistently on multi-step reasoning? Does it excel on product questions but fumble on policy edge cases? These patterns point to dataset gaps or prompt weaknesses.

Third layer — and this is where the real insight lives — worst-performing examples. Sort by lowest score and read the actual responses. You'll spot patterns the aggregate numbers can't show you: the model invents product features that don't exist, it switches tone mid-response, it misunderstands negation in questions. Teresa Torres documented this process for Product Talk's Interview Coach — the systematic failures she found by reading low-scoring examples drove her entire next iteration of prompts and knowledge base structure.

sections.title: Start with the bottom ten
sections.content: When you first look at eval results, ignore the summary stats. Sort by score ascending and read the ten worst responses. You'll learn more in ten minutes than an hour of staring at dashboards. Look for what the failures have in common — that's your next sprint.

sections.sentence: Strong LLM judges achieve 80-90% agreement with humans on general tasks, but only ___% agreement on expert domains requiring specialized knowledge.
sections.explanation: LLM-as-judge performance drops significantly in specialized domains. While general tasks like tone or coherence see 80-90% human agreement, expert domains (medical advice, legal reasoning, advanced technical content) drop to 60-70%. This is why you pair LLM judges for scalable screening with human review for high-stakes or specialized decisions.

sections.title: Detecting Regressions: Comparing Against Baselines
sections.content:
Once you've shipped and your eval pipeline is running continuously, the question shifts from 'is this good?' to 'did this get worse?' That's regression detection, and it's where evals earn their keep in production.

You're watching for two kinds of drift. Prompt drift happens when small wording changes accumulate — you tweak the system message to handle edge case A, then adjust it for edge case B, and three months later nobody remembers why it says what it says and performance has quietly degraded. Model drift happens when your upstream provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, whoever) updates their model and your prompts no longer work as well as they used to.

The way you catch both is historical baselines. Run the same eval dataset every week (or after every significant change). Plot the scores over time per criterion. When you see a drop — even a small one, say from 8.2 to 7.8 — that's your signal to investigate. Hamel Husain's Field Guide emphasizes treating evals like regression tests: any drop below your minimum acceptable threshold should block deployment until you understand why.

sections.statement: Evals are primarily pre-launch tests; once a feature ships, continuous evaluation adds little value since the model and prompts are locked in production.
sections.explanation: This is a critical misconception. Continuous evaluation is essential because data distributions change as user behavior evolves, models drift when providers update them, prompts accumulate small tweaks that degrade performance, and edge cases emerge in production that weren't in your test set. Successful teams treat evals as ongoing product investment, running them regularly to catch regressions before users notice.

sections.title: Non-deterministic systems need multiple runs
sections.content: Unlike traditional software tests, AI systems with temperature > 0 produce different outputs for identical inputs. To get stable eval results, either set temperature to zero for reproducibility, or aggregate scores across multiple runs and use confidence intervals to quantify uncertainty. Make sure your sample size is large enough to detect meaningful differences — 20 examples won't cut it.

points: Mean scores hide the story — always examine the distribution, look for bimodal clusters, and identify fat tails of terrible responses.
Read eval results in three layers: mean scores per criterion, patterns across query types or segments, and the actual worst-performing examples.
Regression detection requires historical baselines — run evals continuously to catch prompt drift and model drift before they degrade user experience.
LLM-as-judge works for scalable screening (80-90% human agreement on general tasks) but drops to 60-70% in expert domains, so pair automation with targeted human review.
Non-deterministic systems need multiple runs or temperature zero for reproducibility, plus confidence intervals to know if a score change is real or noise.

flashcards.front: Why is looking only at average eval scores dangerous when assessing AI product readiness?
flashcards.back: Averages hide the distribution. A 7.5 average could mean consistently mediocre responses, or 80% excellent and 20% catastrophic failures. You need to examine the histogram, identify bimodal clusters, and check for fat tails of terrible responses to understand real product quality.

flashcards.front: What are the three layers of reading eval results, from surface to deep?
flashcards.back: 1) Mean scores per criterion (which rubric dimensions are weak). 2) Score distributions and patterns (how failures cluster by query type or segment). 3) Worst-performing examples (reading actual low-scoring responses to spot systematic issues that numbers can't show).

flashcards.front: What's the difference between prompt drift and model drift in production AI systems?
flashcards.back: Prompt drift: small wording changes accumulate over time as you patch edge cases, quietly degrading performance. Model drift: upstream providers update their models and your existing prompts no longer work as well. Both are caught by running evals continuously and comparing against historical baselines.

flashcards.front: What is the agreement rate between strong LLM judges and humans on general tasks vs. expert domains?
flashcards.back: 80-90% agreement on general tasks (tone, coherence, basic helpfulness), but only 60-70% on expert domains requiring specialized knowledge (medical, legal, advanced technical content). This is why you use LLM judges for scalable screening and humans for high-stakes or specialized review.

flashcards.front: How do you handle non-deterministic AI systems when running evals for reproducibility?
flashcards.back: Either set temperature to zero to get consistent outputs for the same input, or aggregate scores across multiple runs and use confidence intervals to quantify uncertainty. Ensure your sample size is large enough to detect meaningful performance differences.

flashcards.front: What should you do first when analyzing a new batch of eval results?
flashcards.back: Sort by score ascending and read the ten worst-performing examples. Look for what the failures have in common — specific query patterns, missing knowledge, tone shifts, or reasoning errors. This reveals systematic issues faster than studying aggregate statistics.

evals-in-pm-interviews.title: Communicating Evals in Interviews: Frameworks and Examples

sections.title: What Interviewers Are Actually Testing
sections.content:
Here's the thing — when an interviewer asks you to "design an eval framework," they're not looking for you to regurgitate textbook definitions. From what I've seen, they're testing three things: whether you can connect metrics to business impact, whether you understand the trade-offs in your choices, and whether you know how to communicate uncertainty without hedging into meaninglessness.

The best PM candidates I've interviewed talk about evals the way they talk about any product decision — as a series of deliberate trade-offs with clear reasoning. They explain why they'd pick LLM-as-judge for initial screening (scalable, 80-90% agreement on general tasks) but escalate specialized domains to humans (60-70% agreement isn't good enough for medical or legal content). They name the failure modes they're worried about and how they'd detect them early.

You're demonstrating product thinking applied to evaluation. That means starting with the use case, not the tools. What does success look like for this AI feature? What would make you pull it from production? How would you know if it's getting worse over time? Answer those, and the technical choices fall into place.

sections.question: You're interviewing for a PM role at a company building a customer support chatbot. The interviewer asks: "How would you design an eval strategy for this product?" Walk through your framework — what would you say?
sections.sample_answer: I'd start by identifying the core business metrics this chatbot needs to move — likely resolution rate, time to resolution, and customer satisfaction. Then I'd define evaluation criteria that ladder up to those: accuracy (does it answer the question correctly), safety (does it violate policies or hallucinate), and tone (is it empathetic and appropriate). I'd set minimum acceptable scores for each — say accuracy >85%, safety >95% — where falling below any threshold means we don't ship. For sourcing the eval dataset, I'd pull production logs to reflect real user queries, supplement with red-teaming for edge cases, and use human annotation to establish ground truth. I'd run continuous evals to catch drift and examine worst-performing examples to identify systematic failures, not just track average scores.
key_points: Connect evaluation metrics to specific business KPIs (resolution rate, satisfaction, etc.)
Define multiple criteria with minimum thresholds for each dimension
Source eval datasets from production logs plus adversarial cases
Plan for continuous evaluation to detect drift, not just pre-launch testing
sections.explanation: Strong answers demonstrate you think about evals as product strategy, not just technical testing. Interviewers want to see you connect technical metrics to business outcomes, acknowledge trade-offs (human vs automated evaluation, speed vs accuracy), and plan for ongoing iteration rather than one-time validation.

sections.title: The Three-Part Framework That Actually Works
sections.content:
I've watched dozens of PM candidates stumble through eval questions, and the ones who nail it follow a simple pattern. They structure their answer around evaluation strategy, failure mode analysis, and trade-off decisions. That's it. Let me break down what each piece looks like in practice.

Evaluation strategy means naming the criteria that matter for your use case and explaining why. For a trip-planning AI agent, you'd care whether responses answer the user's question (relevance), whether they hallucinate destinations or prices not in your knowledge base (factuality), and whether tone stays helpful across hundreds of test cases (consistency). Notice how each criterion ties directly to user experience — you're not picking metrics because they sound smart.

Failure mode analysis is where you show you've thought about what goes wrong. You'd say: "I'd examine the worst-performing examples in each criterion to find patterns — maybe the agent struggles with budget constraints, or maybe it hallucinates when the knowledge base lacks data." This tells the interviewer you know distributions matter more than averages. A model with 90% average accuracy but systematic failures on a specific query type is a ticking time bomb.

Trade-off decisions close the loop. You'd explain: "I'd use an LLM-as-judge for initial screening across 500 test cases to get fast signal, then have humans review the bottom 10% and a random sample of the rest to calibrate." You're balancing speed, cost, and quality — and you're naming the compromise explicitly. Aman Khan, who runs the evals course with Andrew Ng, calls this "making your assumptions legible" — the interviewer can see your reasoning even if they'd choose differently.

sections.title: Interview Shortcut
sections.content: When you're stuck on an eval question, ask yourself: What would make me pull this feature from production? That failure condition becomes your most important evaluation criterion. Work backward from there.

sections.question: You're explaining your eval approach for a code generation assistant in an interview. You propose using pass@1 (success on first try) as a key metric. The interviewer asks why not just use pass@5 (success within 5 attempts). What's the strongest reasoning for prioritizing pass@1?

options.text: Pass@5 is technically harder to implement and would slow down our testing pipeline
Pass@1 directly reflects the user experience — developers want code that works immediately, not after multiple iterations
Pass@1 gives lower scores, which makes it easier to show improvement over time in stakeholder presentations
Industry benchmarks primarily use pass@1, so it makes our model easier to compare with competitors

sections.explanation: The strongest answer connects the metric to user value. Pass@1 matters because it measures the actual developer experience — getting working code on the first attempt versus needing multiple tries. Option A focuses on implementation convenience (weak), option C is about optics rather than substance, and option D defers to benchmarks without explaining why the metric itself is meaningful. Good interview answers always ladder metrics back to user or business impact.

sections.title: Walking Through a Real Example
sections.content:
Let me show you what this looks like with a concrete case. Teresa Torres documented the eval design for Product Talk's Interview Coach AI, and it's a great model for how PMs should talk through their thinking in interviews.

She started with the business goal: help PMs practice interview skills and get useful feedback. That led to four evaluation criteria — does the coach ask relevant follow-up questions, does it provide actionable feedback, does it avoid hallucinating frameworks or concepts, and does it maintain an encouraging tone? Notice she didn't pick "accuracy" or "fluency" — she picked dimensions that directly serve users learning to interview better.

For the dataset, she sourced real transcripts from practice sessions (production distribution), added edge cases where users give very short or evasive answers (stress-testing), and had experienced PM coaches annotate quality. She set minimum thresholds: feedback quality >85%, safety >95%. Any criterion below threshold meant they weren't shipping that version.

Here's the part that makes this a strong interview answer — she named the ongoing evaluation plan. Continuous eval runs every time they update the prompt or switch models, comparing current scores against historical baselines to catch drift. She also built a feedback loop: users can flag bad responses, which get added to the eval dataset. The eval framework isn't static; it evolves with the product. When you walk through an example like this in an interview, you're showing you think about evals as a living product investment, not a one-time gate.

sections.title: The Feedback Loop
sections.content: The best eval frameworks create a flywheel: production traces inform your datasets, datasets power your evaluations, and evaluations drive product improvements. In interviews, describing this cycle shows you understand evals as continuous iteration, not pre-launch testing.

sections.question: Match each part of a strong interview eval answer to the question it addresses:

pairs.right: What metrics matter for this use case and why?
What patterns appear in worst-performing examples?
How do you balance speed, cost, and quality in evaluation?
How do you detect drift and regression over time?

sections.explanation: Strong interview answers follow this structure because it mirrors how PMs actually work: define success criteria, anticipate what goes wrong, make explicit trade-offs, and plan for iteration. Each component answers a specific question interviewers are testing — not just "do you know evals exist" but "can you apply them to ship better products."

sections.title: Sample Answer Fragment
sections.content: When asked about evaluating a recommendation engine, you might say: "I'd start with business metrics — are we moving engagement and retention? Then I'd define eval criteria: relevance (does the user interact with recommendations), diversity (are we showing varied content or getting stuck in filter bubbles), and freshness (are we surfacing new items). I'd source the eval dataset from historical user interactions, holding out a test set to measure predictive accuracy. For trade-offs, I'd run automated evals daily to catch drift, but have humans review edge cases quarterly to ensure our rubric still reflects what good recommendations look like as user behavior evolves."

points: Interviewers test whether you connect metrics to business impact, understand trade-offs, and communicate uncertainty clearly.
Structure your answer around evaluation strategy (what metrics and why), failure mode analysis (patterns in poor performers), and trade-off decisions (speed vs accuracy, human vs automated review).
Always tie evaluation criteria directly to user experience or business goals — avoid picking metrics because they sound technical.
Emphasize continuous evaluation to detect drift and regression, not just pre-launch testing — evals are a living product investment.
Name your trade-offs explicitly: LLM-as-judge for scalable screening, humans for nuanced high-stakes judgments; examine distributions and worst cases, not just average scores.

flashcards.front: What three things do interviewers test when they ask you to design an eval framework for an AI product?
flashcards.back: Whether you can connect metrics to business impact, whether you understand the trade-offs in your choices, and whether you can communicate uncertainty without hedging. They want to see product thinking applied to evaluation, not textbook definitions.

flashcards.front: What's the three-part framework for answering eval questions in PM interviews?
flashcards.back: Evaluation strategy (what metrics matter for the use case and why), failure mode analysis (identifying patterns in worst-performing examples), and trade-off decisions (balancing speed vs accuracy, automation vs human review). This mirrors how PMs actually work.

flashcards.front: Why should you examine worst-performing examples in your eval results, not just average scores?
flashcards.back: Because distributions matter more than means. A model with 90% average accuracy but systematic failures on a specific query type is a product risk. Patterns in failures guide targeted improvements and help you catch issues before they hit users.

flashcards.front: What's the eval feedback loop (flywheel) you should describe in interviews?
flashcards.back: Production traces inform your eval datasets, datasets power your evaluations, and evaluations drive product improvements. Describing this cycle shows you understand evals as continuous iteration, not one-time pre-launch testing.

flashcards.front: When should you use LLM-as-judge vs human evaluation in your eval framework?
flashcards.back: Use LLM judges for scalable initial screening (80-90% agreement on general tasks), then escalate to humans for nuanced, high-stakes, or specialized contexts (where LLM agreement drops to 60-70%). Name this trade-off explicitly in interviews.

flashcards.front: If you're stuck on an eval question in an interview, what's the shortcut question to ask yourself?
flashcards.back: What would make me pull this feature from production? That failure condition becomes your most important evaluation criterion. Work backward from there to define metrics, thresholds, and monitoring strategy.
